doc.title: Ada Rovatti interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 13, 2022

title: Being a woman jazz musician and Me Too
summary: She discusses tokenism, her mixed feelings on current movements, and the tassel joke.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Wonderful. You know in a perfect world the idea of the woman jazz musician wouldn’t be an issue. Like you’re a jazz musician. But I guess we’re not at that point yet. Have you experienced not getting work that you thought you would have — how do I phrase this? Do you think you’ve lost work because you are a woman jazz musician?

Well I have mixed feelings about all these movements about you know women. Because yes we have been discriminated for a long time. But okay let’s start with the fact yes, we are still seen as kind of like, you know, the beard woman. The circus little gimmick. So, and you know, so festivals say, “Hey we already have a female saxophone player so we cannot hire you.” It’s like, “Yeah but you have 15 male saxophone players.” So sometimes we are still seen as something like a token. At the festivals they need to have a certain amount of women so let’s get one saxophone player, one trumpet. So we are not still kind of just — yeah the other female saxophone player, she’s doing that and I’m doing something else. So even if we are doing the same things we are two different entities playing our own things. Nobody would have thought about saying oh we have Stan Getz and da-da-da-da on it. But we still pay that. The same for magazines, the same

for reviews, the same for a lot of things. Of course some counterpoints say yeah but you know a lot of times in private events they want a girl playing saxophone because it’s cool. Yeah but you know it’s just like it’s minimal. You know you still need to be able to perform you know. So you know, and all the other things it’s like on the other side just to kind of like I don’t know how to straight out the way I’m thinking you know. I found that sometimes you know there is a little too much fear of saying anything these days about women. I did — I grew up with one brother and two cousins so I was kind of I would wrestle them and I never thought a difference between you know, the gender. And when, especially the last couple of years I remember I did a big band gig and the band leader told the main musicians how to dress. And then it was me and another female and he said, “I would never dare to tell you what to wear.” And I thought it was just like Jesus are we like that that we are afraid to even talk about it or just everybody is so, now, like afraid to say half the things — nobody can do a compliment to a woman out of afraid that he’s going to be sued or stuff like that. And I find it’s just a little too far you know. So I remember that I sent back to everyone — I’m twisted, sorry — but I sent to everyone in the big band a big picture of a tassel. A tassel.

And I say, “I was thinking to wear this, is it okay?” You know. Just kind of like okay, loosen up. It’s okay. Maybe it’s my Italian way, I’m a little right on your face about things you know. And I’m pro-women, pro-Me Too movement but let’s also not forget that the camaraderism of a big band, of playing together, of just doing a funny comment. Don’t be afraid. If somebody say, “Oh you cut your hair, you look great.” “Thank you.” Or “You’re wearing that one, you look great in that dress.” “Thank you.” You know? Just let’s not bring it right away — you know I’ve done scenarios that men, they’re looking at their shoes now. They don’t even want to interact out of fear of being out of line as they call it. Yes, we have a long way to go, there is a lot of messed up things. But you know I want to play music. I don’t want to just be bombarded of not the rest of the band talking to me out of fear that, you know, they are not politically correct. That’s my other side. So probably I’m going to get trashed by a lot of women.
